title: Italian Center Attack
description: An excellent opening for beginners and intermediates, relying on an early central attack. Pair with the Fried Liver course.

r1b1k2r/pppp1p1p/3n1n2/3P4/8/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
Black recaptures on f6 with the knight.

Let's give the check we were planning! The lack of Black's dark-squared bishop is apparent here, and Black's queenside is also heavily underdeveloped.

r1b1k2r/pppp1p1p/3n4/3P4/4n3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
This is the only move which keeps equality, but it is played only in 14% of the games.

We'll add pressure to this pinned knight.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pQp/3n1q2/3P4/4n3/2P2N2/P4P.text:
Black defends with ...Qf8.

The queen trade is more or less forced here, as there are no real safe squares for our queen (13.Qg4? runs into ...h5!)

After Black recaptures, we'll be able to generate counterplay with Re1+.

r1b1k2r/pppp3p/3n4/3P1p2/4n3/2P2P2/P2N2P.text:
We'll regain the piece. 

After a few trades on e4, White will be left with a slightly better bishop than Black. 

But it's nearly an endgame with opposite-colored bishops, so this position maintains its equality.

r1b1k2r/ppppBppp/8/8/2BP4/5N2/P4PPP/b2Q2.text:
Here, once the bishops on e7 and a1 come off the board, the material is approximately equal by point count, but the position isn't equal at all. 

Our pieces are MUCH more active than Black's, and White's queen should coordinate with the minor pieces to wreak havoc against Black's open king. These factors should be decisive in this position.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/8/2BP4/B4N2/P4PPP/b2Q.text:
Black captures with the queen.

Now it's time to capture the queen.

r1b2k1r/pp1p2pp/2np1q2/3Q2N1/8/2P5/P4PPP.text:
The queen prevents us from delivering a checkmate.

Re3! is a strong rook lift, threatening Rf3 to pin the queen to the king.

r1b2k1r/pp1p2pp/3p1q2/3Qn1N1/5P2/2P1R3/P.text:
f4 kicks the knight out from e5. 

After the knight moves, we'll double up the rooks on the e-file and continue hunting down the king!

r1b2k1r/pppp1p1p/3n1n2/3P4/8/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
...Kf8 is a huge mistake, but played nearly a whopping 70% of the time!

We can play Bh6+! to set up a mating net.

r1b3kr/pppp1p1p/3n1n1B/3PR3/8/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
And Rg5+ is a serious threat, which is hard to defend.

Black could go for ...Ne4 to stop Rg5+, but then we have Nh4 with f3 coming to kick it out.

r1bq1k1r/pp1p2pp/2np4/3Q2b1/8/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black gets rid of the pressure on the bishop by trading it off.

Of course, we would never trade queens here. We'll recapture with the knight, which comes with a checkmate threat.

r1bq1k1r/pp1pb1pp/2np4/3Q2B1/8/2P2N2/P4P.text:
Black supports the bishop on e7 by retreating the knight. The knight was also loose on a5, leading to possible tactics if Black's queen was deflected.

It is time to bring the a1 rook into the game.

r1bq1k1r/pp1pb1pp/3p4/n2Q4/8/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
The king retreats to f8.

Now for another key move: we bring the dark-squared bishop to g5, further pressuring Black's pieces and allowing the rook on a1 to join the attack as well.

r1bq3r/pp1pbkpp/3p4/n7/8/2P2N2/P4PPP/R1B.text:
Black recaptures.

Let's bring the queen into the attack with check!

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
3...Bc5 is the second most popular move in this position (after ...Nf6), played in nearly 30% of the games.

Black doesn't allow us to go for the Fried Liver Attack, but instead brings the bishop out to c5, with similar intentions as our bishop on c4.

Our recommendation in this course is to immediately play 4.c3, initiating a simple, but powerful idea of a quick d4-push.

r1bqk2r/pp1pbppp/3p4/n7/2B5/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black grabs the pawn on d6.

Now, we can sacrifice our bishop on f7! The purpose of this sacrifice is to lure the king out into the open; Black's minor pieces are very passive, which usually indicates that a piece sacrifice is a correct one in the position.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/3p4/2BP4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black saves the bishop and blocks the check.

We'll save our bishop as well.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bppp/2n5/3p4/3P4/2PB1N2/P4PP.text: This position is equal. Nevertheless, both of our bishops have good diagonals and we have the semi-open b and e-files to work with. White has good compensation for the pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3p4/1bBP4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
This is the engine's top choice, equalizing the position.

We next improve the rook by giving a check on e1.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/b2p4/Q1BP4/B4N2/P4PP.text:
We are threatening d4-d5, so Black attacks our bishop in return while blocking our d-pawn.

However, 13.Bb5 comes and Black's pieces are loose!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2n5/bB1p4/Q2P4/B4N2/P4PP.text: Following ...Bb6, Black's position will fall apart after Bxc6.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/2BP4/B1b2N2/P4PPP.text:
Black blocks the scope of the dark-squared bishop on a3 and intends to castle.

We'll save our rook with tempo, attacking the bishop.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/b7/2BP4/B4N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black retreats to a5.

Now, a key move: our queen can add pressure to the knight and the bishop at the same time.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2b2/3P4/2B1n3/5N2/PP3.text:
Many times, Black saves the bishop with ...Bf6.

Let's line up our rook with the uncastled king.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.text:
Nearly 60% of the games continue with Black bringing the knight to f6.

Now it's time for d4. Note that 5.d3 defending the e-pawn is perfectly playable, but we will be looking at the more forcing and aggressive 5.d4 in this course.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.text:
Black should sensibly trade on d4, as other moves are significantly weaker. This occurs in 90% of the games.

We recapture with the pawn, which comes with an attack on the c5-bishop while maintaining our pawn center.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
The following studies are divided in regards to what Black does in this moment and on the next move.

First, we will look at Bb4+. Black gives a check on b4, which is a move that has been played 75% of the time.

We recommend 7.Nc3 here, a very sharp and active approach that doesn't block our dark-squared bishop.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBP4/2n2N2/PP3PP.text:
This capture occurs close to 45% of the time. Black is likely hoping to relieve the central tension without giving up their bishop pair.

We will simply recapture the knight.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bBPn3/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
Now, 7...Nxe4 is by far the strongest move for Black and also the most common, played almost 60% of the time. Black captures a pawn and piles up on the c3-knight, but that's what we use to our advantage! 

While Black is occupied by the knight on c3, our king gets to safety and prepares Re1+ against the uncastled king!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BP4/2b2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black grabs on c3 yet again and attacks our rook on a1: a very natural-looking move. However, ...Bxc3? actually gives us a big advantage!

First, let's prevent Black from castling by playing Ba3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BP4/B4N2/P4PPP/b.text:
Black's greed doesn't end here and they even capture the rook!

It is time to punish Black's uncastled king and lack of development. White can start by giving a check with the remaining rook.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BPn3/2b2N2/PP3PP.text:
In 47% of the games, Black captures on c3 with the bishop.

We can now gain some space in the center with 9.d5, attacking the knight at the same time.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/3n4/3P4/3Qn3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black saves the knights by retreating to d6.

We can now grab the g7-pawn and attack the rook on h8.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/3P4/2n1n3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
In return, Black gets our light-squared bishop.

To continue playing actively, our next move is Qd4. From d4, the queen has three targets: the pawn on g7 and the knights on e4 and c4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/3Pn3/2B1n3/2b2N2/PP3P.text:
Black immediately saves the knight by jumping to e5 and counter-attacking our c4-bishop.

We'll grab the bishop on c3.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/2n5/8/2BP4/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black plays it "safely" and retreats back to e7.

Now we can gain space with d5 and kick the knight out from c6.

r1bqk2r/ppppbppp/8/n2P4/2B5/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black jumps to a5, attacking our bishop.

Our primary goal should be to open up the e-file against Black's uncastled king. The key move here is thus 11.d6!, also opening up our light-squared bishop, aimed at the soft f7-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/5b2/3P4/2B1R3/5N2/PP3PP.text: Now we have a handful of attacking ideas. Obviously Black is quite solid and smart to reach this far though, so a fight is ahead.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/5b2/3P4/2B1n3/5N2/PP3PP.text:
Black saves the knight on c6.

White simply recaptures on e4.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/8/8/2BP4/B4N2/P4PPP/b2Q.text:
Black can only block with a piece, since the king cannot go to f8.

Let's grab the knight, which is attacked twice by a rook and bishop, but defended by a king and a queen!

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Black develops in a similar way, supporting the pawn on e5.

Next, we will play 3.Bc4 — the signature move of the Italian!

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3P4/1Pp5/5N2/P4PPP/.text: But now we deliver a fork on d5 and win a piece!

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/3p4/1bBP4/2P2N2/P4P.text:
Black keeps the tension on the queenside and blocks the check by playing ...Be6.

This is a mistake, yet it happened in 22% of the games!

Here, we should gladly grab the bishop on b4!

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2n1b3/8/1PpP4/5N2/P4PPP/R.text: Black thinks they've got out of trouble.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
There won't be an Italian game without 1.e4 and 1...e5 on the board!

As usual, our knight will occupy its usual f3-square, attacking e5 and controlling the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the Italian! 

Let's take a look at the Italian Game, where Black brings out the bishop to c5 on the third move (instead of 3...Nf6, allowing us to go for The Fried Liver.)

The following four studies explore White's c3, d4 setup.

Let's check it out!

r1bq1r1k/pppp2p1/3P1np1/4N1p1/2B5/2P5/P4.text: Black's position just collapses after our knight enters a strong outpost on e5, targeting the g6-pawn. The tripled isolated pawns are indefensible, and White's remaining pieces will enter the attack via the h-file.

r1bq1r1k/pppp2p1/3P1np1/6p1/2B5/2P2N2/P4.text: The king moves off the diagonal.

r1bq1r2/ppp2pp1/3p2k1/n1nP2N1/6Q1/2P5/P4.text: Black opens up an attack on our queen...

r1bq1r2/ppp2pp1/3pN1k1/n1nP4/6Q1/2P5/P4P.text: ...but after Ne6+, there will be a checkmate on the next move!

r1bq1r2/pppp1pp1/3n2k1/3P2N1/6Qn/2P5/P4P.text:
But after Qg4 Black's position is hopeless.

Discovered check like Ne6+ or even grabbing the knight on h4 is very powerful here.

r1bq1r2/pppp1pp1/3n2k1/3P2N1/7n/2P5/P4PP.text: Black goes forward to g6, since ...Kg8 runs into Qh5.

r1bq1r2/pppp1pp1/6k1/n1nP2N1/8/2P5/P4PPP.text:
Black steps forward, since ...Kg8 walks into Qh5.

We will now bring the queen into the attack. From g4, it threatens a strong discovered check.

r1bq1r2/pppp1ppk/3n4/3P4/7n/2P2N2/P4PP1/.text:
Black captures.

It's a simple pattern: we follow up with Ng5+ and then bring the queen into the attack.

r1bq1r2/pppp1ppk/8/n1nP4/8/2P2N2/P4PPP/R.text: Bxh7+ works here as well! Black recaptures, and now we can play the typical Greek gift ideas.

r1bq1r2/pppp1ppk/8/n2P4/8/2n2N2/P4PPP/R1.text:
Black captures the bishop.

Be careful not to play Ng5+? here, as Black can sacrifice their queen with ...Qxg5! because our queen is still hanging.

Instead, let's get our queen out of danger with tempo, and involve her in the attack.

r1bq1r2/pppp2p1/6k1/n1nP1pN1/6Q1/2P5/P4P.text:
Black tries to attack our queen.

We can just retreat it to g3 and the threat of Ne6+ is still relevant.

r1bq1r2/pppp2p1/6k1/n1nP1pN1/8/2P3Q1/P4P.text:
There is no good way for Black to prevent massive material loss from the knight and queen's discovered attacks.

If Black tries to run with ...Kf6, we can play Be3 and continue involving pieces into the attack. We also always have the fork with Nh7+ in our back pocket. Black is toast.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1pp1/1p3n1B/n2P4/7Q/2PB1N2/.text:
...so let's play Bxh6 instead! 

Black cannot recapture on h6, since they cannot bring enough forces from the queenside to defend their weak king.

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1pp1/1p3n1p/n2P4/7Q/2PB1N2/.text: Black prevents us from adding pressure to the knight by playing Bg5...

r1bq1rk1/p1pp1ppp/1p3n2/n2P4/Q7/2PB1N2/P.text:
Black supports the knight.

The real purpose of Qa4 was to swing the queen over to the kingside to support our attack.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/5nn1/3P2pP/2B5/2P2N2/P.text:
Black takes the bishop which was pinning their f6-knight.

We can take a piece too, but our capture has much graver strategic consequences for Black's position.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/5nnp/3P2B1/2B4P/2P2N2/.text:
Black attacks our bishop in return.

But we can just keep advancing! Black can't take on h5 because the f6 knight is pinned to the queen.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/8/n2P2N1/8/2nQ4/P4PPP/.text: If Black goes for ...f5 or ...g6, we can shift the queen to h3 and threaten a checkmate from there.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1pp1/8/n2P4/8/2nQ1N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black retreats the king.

We can now bring the knight in to threaten a checkmate on h7.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
This move is played about 15% of the time, and Black immediately moves the king out of the center.

We'll do the same, temporarily sacrificing the pawn on e4, but the king's safety is more important here, as Black can have many tactics along the e-file.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/2BPP3/2b2N2/PP.text:
Black goes for the e4-pawn by trading away its defender. This is an intentional gambit on our part.

We recapture the bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BPn3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black grabs the e4 pawn.

Now, the thematic move: d5! We aggressively displace Black's knight, and also prevent Black from playing d5 themselves, which would solve a lot of their problems.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/3n2n1/3P4/8/2PB1N2/P4P.text:
Black blocks the view of the bishop.

Now, h4! is an aggressive move, intending to kick away he knight from g6.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/3n4/3P4/7n/2PB1N2/P4PP.text:
Black captures on h4, since their queen is also looking over that square.

But the Greek Gift sacrifice works here as well!

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/5n2/n2P4/8/2PB1N2/P4PP.text:
In 34% of the games, the knight retreats to f6 here.

Black's loose knight on a5 gives us the opportunity to activate our queen with tempo.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/5nn1/3P2B1/2B5/2P2N2/P.text:
Black supports the knight by opening up the queen, although this means the knight is pinned.

Time to target the knight on g6 again! h2-h4 is the classic way to do this.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/n1nP4/8/2PB1N2/P4PPP.text:
Nearly 30% of the time, Black brings the knight to c5 and tries to get our bishop from there.

What might the best move be, considering Black's poor queenside development?

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/n2P4/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4P.text:
The most popular move, occurs in nearly half of the games. Black tries to get rid of our strong light-squared bishop.

We'll retreat it to d3 and counterattack the e4 knight.
...Nxc3, ...Nf6, and ...Nc5 are the most popular moves, and they all losing! Only ...f5 holds.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/n2P4/8/2nB1N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black grabs a second pawn, unaware of the danger in the position.

Qe1 or Qd2 would skewer the knights and win a piece, but even better is the Greek gift sacrifice! Once again, Black's queenside development is non-existent, which indicates that a sacrifice on the other side of the board is likely sound.

r1bq1rk1/pppp2p1/5np1/3P2p1/2B5/2P2N2/P4.text:
Black recaptures on g6. The g6-pawn and the light-squared bishop had a nice interplay aimed at the f7-pawn.

Now, we have an excellent discovered check to play.

r1bq1rk1/ppppnppp/3n4/3P4/2B5/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
In 60% of the the knight retreats to safety on d6 and attacks our bishop. However, this blocks the d-pawn, which hinders their development in the long term.

We'll tuck it back the bishop, once again eyeing the h7-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/ppppnppp/5n2/3P4/2B5/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
In a quarter of the games, Black retreats the knight to f6.

The thematic move when Black's knight is on f6 is Bg5; we add pressure to the knight, and here we threaten to double the f-pawns in front of Black's king.

r1bq1rk1/ppppnppp/8/3P4/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
In 39% of the games, Black retreats the knight to e7.

White can add pressure along the e-file with their rook.

r1bq1rkn/pppp1pp1/5n1p/3P2BP/2B5/2P2N2/P.text: Black tries to play defensively by retreating the knight back to h8.

r1bq1rkn/pppp1pp1/5n1p/3P3P/2B4B/2P2N2/P.text: By retreating the bishop we maintain the pin on f6 and try to make use of Black's heavy underdevelopment.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text:
Again, 3...Bc5 develops and avoids the Fried Liver.

As you saw in the last study, our recommendation here is to play for a quick c2-c3 and d2-d4 push.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.text:
Black brings the knight out and pressures the e4-pawn.

We can now expand with d4 as it is well-supported.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.text: Black trades, and we will recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.text: Black gives a check on b4, and the line recommend here is to block with Nc3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text: Both knights are developed again, and now we will play 3.Bc4 to enter the Italian.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/4P3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text: As always, we begin with 1.e4 e5, and then look to develop normally.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The second study analyses 7...O-O. 

Black doesn't capture the pawn on e4, but gets their king into safety instead. 

Let's check it out!

r1b1k2r/pppp1ppp/8/n1qP4/8/2nB1N2/P2Q1PP.text: Black covers the knights with the queen.

r1b1k2r/pppp1ppp/8/n1qP4/8/2nB1N2/PB1Q1P.text:
And now we fianchetto the bishop to b2, adding another attacker to Black's c3-knight.

The pawn on g7 is also very loose, and with Re1+ coming, White is doing great here.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/n2P4/8/2nB1N2/P2Q1PPP.text:
Black gives a check on e7. This is necessary to bring the queen to c5 to defend both knights.

We should not trade queens and give up our active play, so we move the king to f1! Black still has problems dealing with their hanging knights.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/5n2/n2P4/8/2PB1N2/P4PP.text: Black castles as well, and the position has transposed into a line from the previous study.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/5n2/n2P4/Q7/2PB1N2/P4P.text: And we've arrived at an already familiar position, where we first attack the knight on a5 and next slide the queen to h4 to initiate a strong attack!

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text: The bishops are developed to their typical Italian squares, and now White will commence the plan of immediately playing c2-c3 and d2-d4.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.text:
Black brings the knight out and pressures the e4-pawn.

We can now expand with d4 as it is well-supported.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.text: As in the last two studies, Black trades, and we will recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3P.text: Black gives a check on b4, and the line recommended here is to block with Nc3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/2BPP3/2b2N2/PP3.text: Previously we have looked at 7...O-O, but in this line, Black takes on c3, removing the defender of e4 and intending to grab the pawn. This is played in approximately 15% of games.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2BPn3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
Grabbing some material here and breaking down some of White's center is most sensible as Black. In many positions, if White was allowed to play e4-e5 or d4-d5, it would be very annoying for Black.

Typically in this opening, after we sacrifice the e-pawn for development, we CANNOT allow d7-d5, which would stabilize Black's position. Thus, we should play d5 ourselves.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/n2P4/8/2PB1N2/P4PPP.text:
The knight retreats back to f6 instead of grabbing the d5-pawn, which would give White active development.

Here, we can simply castle.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/n2P4/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
40% of the time, Black jumps to a5 and attacks our bishop on c4.

This is very similar to the previous study where both players have inserted O-O. As before, we should retreat the bishop to d3 with tempo.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/n2P4/8/2nB1N2/P4PPP/R.text:
Black goes for even more material and captures another pawn. In the previous study where both sides castled, we had the Greek gift sacrifice in this position.

Here, on the other hand, it is good enough to play Qd2, skewering the knights. We don't mind blocking the dark-squared bishop for now, since it will be fianchettoed to b2 later anyway.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/5n2/3P2B1/2BQ4/2P2N2/P4.text: There is no good way for Black to defend against Bxf6 without further contorting their position. White will often regain the pawn here with positional interest, since Black's kingside pawns will be weak, and their king will be unsafe.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/5n2/3P4/2BQ4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black saves both the knight and the pawn, but at the cost of another tempo that they aren't spending developing.

White should continue developing actively with Bg5, threatening to cripple Black's pawn structure.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/8/3P4/2B1n3/2P2N2/P4PPP.text:
In close to 30% of the games, Black went for ...Ne7.

Since Black hasn't castled here, the g7-pawn is unprotected, and our queen can find a nice square on d4, from where it attacks both the g7-pawn and the knight on e4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text: Both knights are developed to their natural squares.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
This study delves into yet another of Black's 7th moves, which is ...Bxc3.

Let's get right into it!

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/1bP5/8/2B5/5N2/PP2QnPP/.text:
Black blocks with the queen, as they don't want to lose the castling rights with ...Kf8.

We can throw in another check here by capturing on d7, thus avoiding losing the pawn on c6.

r1bq1k1r/pp1p1ppp/1bnP4/8/2B3n1/5N2/PP2Q.text:
Black sidesteps their king.

It is finally time to castle, so we get the king into safety and also protect the pawn on f2.

If Black allows it, we can go for a tactical shot with Bxf7, since after Ng5+, Black's knight on g4 will be hanging.

Regardless, Black's position is miserable due to their stranded king, lack of development, and terrible piece coordination.

r1bq1k1r/ppppnBpp/1b1P4/4P1B1/8/1Q3N2/PP.text:
And after Bg5, there is tremendous pressure against the e7-knight, ensuring that we'll win Black's queen!

Our opponent's lack of coordination and development is yet again fatal.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text: The bishops are developed to their typical Italian squares, and now White will commence the plan of immediately playing c2-c3 and d2-d4.

r1bqk2r/pp1p1ppp/1bnP4/8/2B3n1/5N2/PP3PP.text:
Black returns the knight to c6.

It's time to continue working to keep Black's king in the center. Qe2+! forces Black to surrender castling rights.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnppp/1b1p4/4P3/2B3n1/5N2/PP3.text:
Black can ignore f2 for now and trades on d6.

We'll gladly recapture with the pawn, and attack the knight yet again.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bP5/8/2B5/5N2/PP3nPP/R.text: Black delivers a fork. Now, it is time to counterattack, starting by getting the queen out of danger with tempo.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/2BPP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
In 16% of the games, the bishop retreats to b6, which already gives White some advantage. 

Nevertheless, it could get a bit tricky to play this correctly as White. In general, we should try to quickly roll Black over by advancing the pawn center; in that vein, the move here is d4-d5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn5/3P4/2B1n3/5N2/PP3P.text:
This happens very rarely (only in 5% of the games in the database), as Black is sacrificing a piece on c6 and aggressively hunting our f2-pawn.

Black's attacking forces aren't enough, so we should simply accept the material.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2.text:
Black brings the knight out and pressures the e4-pawn.

We can now expand with d4 as it is well-supported.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/P.text: As in the previous studies, Black trades, and we will recapture with the pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/1b1P4/4P3/2B5/1Q3N2/PP3.text: The queen-bishop battery creates a higher level threat against the f7-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/1b1P4/4P3/2B5/5N2/PP3nP.text: Black captures on f2, going for the fork.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/1b3n2/3P4/2B1P3/5N2/PP3.text:
In 35% of the games, Black retreats the knight to e7. e4 is still hanging, but notice that our pieces defend d5 twice.

Thus, we can continue gaining space and disrupting Black's setup with e5!

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/1b6/3PP3/2B3n1/5N2/PP3P.text:
Black doesn't passively retreat to g8, but jumps to g4 instead, adding another attacker to f2.

It's time to push again! We don't have to worry about f2. Black doesn't have enough firepower to generate a successful attack. Meanwhile, d5-d6 opens up our light-squared bishop aimed at the weak f7-pawn.

r1bqk2r/ppppnppp/3P4/4P3/2B3n1/5N2/PP3bP.text:
...Kf1 and suddently all of Black's pieces are loose!

We'll win at least one of them.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text: Both knights are developed to their natural squares.

r3k2r/pppbqppp/1b6/8/2B5/5N2/PP2QnPP/RNB.text:
The bishop recaptures.

Remember that we are up significant material, so it is now very acceptable to trade queens.

r6r/pppbkppp/1b6/8/2B5/5N2/PP3nPP/RNB1K2.text: After Black recaptures, we can save the rook by attacking the knight and threatening to win two pieces for a rook.

r6r/pppbkppp/1b6/8/2B5/5N2/PP3nPP/RNB1KR.text: The position is a bit strange, but White is clearly on top with the extra piece. Natural development will continue with moves like Nc3 and Bg5, and as long as White doesn't blunder material, they should be able to easily take over the endgame.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to the fourth study! 

Here, Black abandons the plan of giving a check on b4 (6...Bb4+) and goes for ...Bb6, which is already a bad move.

Let's check out how to punish it!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/6B1/1bBPP3/2N2N2.text:
This pin is powerful because of our Nd5 and Qd3 ideas. 

We've got moves to increase the pressure, but also to develop all our pieces and support our center. 

Black will have a tough time fighting our central pawn duo.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/P.text: If the main line is avoided and Black castles, we'll go 9.Bg5.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/1bnp4/4p3/2BPP3/2P2N2/P.text:
Less than 10% of games continue with ...Bb6; Black retreats the bishop and hopes to keep it exerting pressure on our dark squares.

After 6.dxe5, we are almost always simply winning a pawn. Most games (about 80%) continue with 6...Nxe5 or 6...dxe5, but both of those moves are terrible, since after trading queens, either the e5 or f7 pawns drop at the end of the line.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/1bnp4/8/2BPP3/5N2/PP3PP.text:
This move here is played in a more favorable move order. 

The reason is that Black has inserted ...exd4 and so they won't be left with the problem of dxe5.

We'll play Bb5, which threatens to win the pinned c6-knight with d5.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b1p3/2B1P3/2P2N2/.text:
A move played about 25% of the time is 4...d6 to lend e5 some more support. This move is significantly less active than ...Nf6, since Black is not pressuring our e-pawn as in other lines.

d2-d4 is still the clear continuation here, expanding and breaking in the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b5/2BpP3/2P2N2/PP.text: Most of the time you'll see Black simply trade pawns, but we don't mind seeing this. After our c3-pawn recaptures, we will have two strong pawns in the center.

r1bqk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/1bBPP3/5N2/PP3PP.text:
Check! This is played half of the time in the database, but it isn't that good.

We block and develop with Nc3, and in this move order, Black has not played ...Nf6 and thus cannot win our e-pawn.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1p3/2B1P3/5N2/PP.text: The bishops are developed to their typical Italian squares, and now White will commence the plan of immediately playing c2-c3 and d2-d4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/1bBPP3/2N2N2/PP.text:
It's quite possible that we could have a transposition with this move order.

We'll castle.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text: Both knights are developed to their natural squares.

r2q1knr/pp3ppp/1b1p4/1B2n3/4P1b1/2P2N2/P.text:
If Black is stubborn and they don't want to block the check, they'll have to lose castling rights.

Now, we can bring the bishop back to break the pin.

r2q1knr/pp3ppp/1b1p4/4n3/4P1b1/2P2N2/PP2.text: Up a pawn with a better position, all we must do now is finish development. Na3 and Nc2 is a good maneuver to then pivot to e3.

r2q1rk1/pppb1ppp/1bnp1n2/1B6/3PP3/2N2N1P.text:
And here we prevent ...Bg4. 

We want to play moves Re1 and maybe even e5 to attack the f6-knight. 

We've got a clear advantage thanks to our two central pawns.

r2q1rk1/pppbnppp/1bnp4/1B6/3PP3/2N2N1P/P.text: But again, we prevent ...Bg4 and we will continue with Re1 and moves like Be3.

r2qk1nr/pp3ppp/1b1p4/4n3/2B1P1b1/2P2N2/P.text:
Perhaps Black's only idea to create counterplay, but it doesn't work. 

9.Be2 is also fine, but even better is throwing in a check while saving the bishop.

r2qk1nr/pp3ppp/1bnp4/8/2B1P1b1/2P2N2/PP3.text:
Most players simply recapture on d6, not knowing d6 becomes a weakness and that they lose valuable time.

White should now castle, bringing their king to safety and enjoying their extra pawn and better position.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/1bnp4/4P3/2B1P1b1/2P2N2/.text:
Bg4, the best move, is only played in around 13% of games in the database. The best move for White here is to chop on d6 and grab the extra pawn.

Note that 6...Bg4 is only roughly equal after 7.exd6 Nf6!?, with very strange complications. The majority of players aren't aware of these dynamics.

r2qk1nr/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/1bBPP1b1/2N2N2/PP.text:
The bishop pins our f3-knight.

We can simply castle here and start using our lead in development to cause problems for Black.

r2qk1nr/pppb1ppp/1bnp4/1B6/3PP3/5N2/PP3P.text:
Black unpins.

Now Nc3 develops further and supports our center. 

The short-term plan is simple: h3 and castling.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/1bBPP1b1/2N2N2/P.text:
Black develops the knight and pressures e4. The position seems stable for Black, but it actually is not.

Now Nd5! is a tricky move: we can attack the bishop, and all the continuations favor White.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/3P4/1bBP4/5P2/PP3P1P.text: The double isolated pawns are a bit ugly, but they are a small price to pay for White's imminent material gain.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/3P4/1bBP4/5b2/PP3PPP.text: Black may try and take on f3, but we won't recapture with the queen.

r2qk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/3n4/1bBPP1b1/5N2/PP3.text: For instance if Black trades, we open the e-file with tempo. More importantly, once the c6 knight is deflected, we will have Qa4+, winning the bishop.

r2qk2r/pppb1ppp/1bnp1n2/1B6/3PP3/2N2N2/P.text:
The knight can go on f6. 

But since our knight already defends e4, we can simply castle.

r2qk2r/pppbnppp/1bnp4/1B6/3PP3/2N2N2/PP3.text:
Developing the knight to e7 helps Black a little because if we play e5 it won't attack their knight like in the ...Nf6 line.

We castle.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 2, we analyze 3...Bc5 with other moves.

In this study, the move 4...d6 that protects the e5-pawn will be explored.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/3p1n1p/8/2BQPB1P/2N5/P.text:
10.e5 or 10.f3 were also options, but I like 10.h4 to attack. 

This may make many players with Black nervous, and spend some time thinking of how to defend. 

f3 is an idea that we could also go for later, and Qd2 to sacrifice on h6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1bpp1/3p1n1p/8/2BQPB2/2N5/PP.text: Black castles, but their king is now on a lonely side of the board.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1Bp1/2n4p/2b5/3NP3/8/PPP2PP.text:
With the idea of Qh5+.

If Black doesn't take the bishop, we can simply trade down. White will be up a pawn and will enjoy hunting Black's king, which can no longer castle.

r1bqk1nr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/2b5/2BNP3/8/PPP2P.text: This move loses on the spot.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1pp1/2p2n1p/8/1bB1P3/2N5/PPP.text:
The b-pawn recaptures.

We should castle now. With our king in safety, it'll be harder to win a pawn on e4.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1pp1/2p2n1p/8/2B1P3/2b5/PPP2.text:
Black takes. They may feel like they have to at this point.

After recapturing, our plan is to play e5 to dislodge the knight. It's dangerous for Black to take on e4.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1pp1/2p4p/8/2B1n3/2P5/P1P2PP.text: If they take on e4, we have some ways to create problems.

r1bqk2r/p1pp1pp1/2p4p/8/2B1n3/B1P5/P1P2P.text:
We start taking control of the dark squares around the king. We also stop them from castling here. 

The best continuation for Black is 10...d5 11.Bb3 Nd6. But in that case we can attack c6 with 12.Ba4.

r1bqk2r/ppp1bpp1/3p1n1p/8/2BQPB2/2N5/PPP.text:
Black prepares to castle.

We can castle queenside here and use our dominating position to start an attack!

r1bqk2r/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/8/1bBNP3/2N5/PPP.text:
Black pins our knight, and thus rethreatens ...Nxe4.

We can start by trading the other knights and relieving some tension.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2pp1/3p1n1p/8/2BQP3/2N5/PPP2.text:
Black develops the knight.

We can continue developing our pieces with Bf4.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1pp1/2n2n1p/8/2BNP3/8/PPP2P.text:
5...Nf6 attacks e4.

We can defend naturally with 6.Nc3.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2pp1/2np3p/4p3/2BPP3/5N2/PPP.text:
About 12% of games continue with 4...d6. 

Black defends e5, but the simple capture on e5 is good.

r1bqkbnr/ppp2pp1/3p3p/8/2BQP3/8/PPP2PPP/.text:
Black opens up their light-squared bishop. 

Since our position has already been opened thanks to our first moves and d4-pawn break, we can simply continue development with Nc3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/4p3/2B1P3/5N2/PPP.text:
3...h6 is surprisingly played 13% of the time here. At such an early stage of the game, this includes more than 32 million games! 

Still, if the idea is to avoid a Fried Liver at all costs, 3...Bc5 is better.

Because Black has essentially wasted a move, we should strike immediately in the center with d2-d4; there is no reason to prepare it with c3 here.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/2n4p/8/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
About 70% of the games in the database continue like this, with Black opening the position.

We should recapture with the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1pp1/7p/8/2BnP3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
If this capture happens, we've got everything we wanted in the position.

After 6.Qxd4, we have a massive lead in development and unopposed central control.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Both knights are developed to their natural squares.

We play Bc4 here, to enter the Italian.

r2q1rk1/ppp1npp1/2nb2bp/1B6/4P1P1/2N1BN1.text:
We're going to play Qe2, Bd3 in some variations if we need to defend e4, and castle queenside.

Rg1 is also an idea to push our kingside pawns. White stands better due to the space advantage and the extra pawn.

r2q1rk1/ppp1npp1/2nb2bp/1B6/4P1P1/2N2N1P.text:
The bishop retreats to g6. 

There's some pressure on e4, but it's currently defended.

r2q1rk1/ppp1npp1/2nb3p/1B5b/4P3/2N2N1P/P.text:
Black castles. ...Ne5 is enabled.

It is time to play g4. There won't be significant weaknesses that Black will be able to take advantage of, especially since we haven't castled yet. This expansion lets us play actively and aggressively.

r2qk1nr/ppp2pp1/2nb3p/7b/2B1P3/5N1P/PPP2.text:
If they keep the pin, that's fine. 

Our plan will be to play g4 later.

First, though, we can pin their knight to avoid Ne5.

r2qk1nr/ppp2pp1/2nb3p/8/2B1P1b1/5N2/PPP2.text:
The bishop recaptures. 

It's more active on the d6-square in this line because it helps control the center.

We should start by forcing Black to making a choice with the light-squared bishop.

r2qk2r/ppp1npp1/2nb3p/1B5b/4P3/5N1P/PPP2.text:
Black supports their knight with the other one.

We have some time to develop here. Nc3 supports our center.

r2qkbnr/ppp2pp1/2np3p/4P3/2B1P1b1/5N2/PP.text:
Black recaptures on e5 in 80% of games. In the previous 3...Bc5 lines, we saw that recapturing the pawn on e5 is lost due to Qxd8+ and Bxf7! ideas. 

The only move to save the game is once again ...Bg4, and even then, the defense is not obvious. In less than 20% of games, players managed to find this move.

Obviously, we can now take on d6 and be up a pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we'll see what to do if Black plays 3...h6 to protect their g5-square.

This move isn't good this early, because it wastes time that they should use in developing pieces.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2nq4/1B1pN3/2PPp3/8/PP3P.text:
We simply are too ahead in development and activity. 

7...dxc4 8.Nc3 attacks e4. 

We will simply be getting turbo development and Black is in trouble. They won't be able to defend everything.

r1b1kbnr/ppp3pp/2nq4/1B1pN3/3Pp3/8/PPP2P.text: Black defends the knight using their queen.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/5p2/2BNP3/8/PPP2P.text:
5...Nf6 covers our queen's checking square.

We'll play 6.Nc3 to support our e4-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp2pp/2n2n2/6B1/2BNp3/2N5/PPP.text:
We have maximum pressure on e4 and by extension on Black's entire position. 

We're going to castle. f3 to open up our rook is also a powerful idea to increase pressure on the knight.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2n5/3pN3/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP.text:
5...d5 is one of the best moves under the circumstances for Black.

We can simply pin the knight.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/4P3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
Both knights are developed to their natural squares.

We play Bc4 here and enter the Italian.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2BnP3/5N2/PPPP1P.text:
This is the Blackburne Gambit. 

If we take on e5, ...Qg5 is good for Black (a famous trap). So instead, we simply trade knights and double Black's pawns.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/8/2BpP3/8/PPPP1PPP/R.text:
And we castle. 

We'll be calm about this, and play slow, improving moves like c3 and Re1.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/4p3/2BPp3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black can take on e4. This is the most popular move.

We can counter by grabbing the pawn on e5, opening up our queen in the process.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/4pp2/2B1P3/5N2/PPPP.text:
This is the Rousseau Gambit. If we accept the pawn, Black gets full compensation and good attacking chances with ...e4.

Instead, we'll push with d4.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/5p2/2BpP3/5N2/PPP2P.text:
Black can also choose to take on d4.

We should recapture with the knight, which also opens up our queen.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4P3/2B1p3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text: It's very hard to stop Qd5. The engine gives us a +2 advantage.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4n3/2BPp3/8/PPP2PPP/R.text:
Black trades knights. 

This is already a huge mistake.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, I want to show you two gambits that Black could try to play! 

We have to learn them to avoid their traps.
